lessons.title: What people mean by “AI”
lessons.html:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a name for computer systems that do tasks people often use thinking for, such as making sense of spoken language, learning from examples, or solving problems. A Government of Canada guide on generative AI uses that kind of plain description.

Generative AI is a type of AI that makes new content. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre) says it creates unique content by learning from large sets of data that were fed into the model. That content can be text, images, audio, video, or computer code. Older, more traditional AI systems often recognize patterns or sort existing content. Generative AI can create something new.

You use generative AI by giving it a short instruction, called a prompt or query. The Government of Canada guide explains that many of these tools produce the next words or images that are statistically likely, based on their training data. The result can look as though a person made it. That does not mean a person checked it, and it does not mean it is true.

People use these tools for everyday things such as drafting a note, summarizing a long page, or making an image. Organizations also use AI in many kinds of work. This course does not say you must use AI, and it does not name or recommend a product.

This course is not a technical certificate. It will not teach you how to build an AI system. The next lessons focus on three practical skills: checking answers, protecting your privacy, and watching for scams.

lessons.title: Check AI answers before you use them
lessons.html:
Generative AI can sound confident even when it is wrong. The Cyber Centre says you should be cautious with information that comes from AI. Its outputs:

  • can be incorrect
  • might not make sense
  • might not take certain factors into account
  • can be biased

The Cyber Centre also says you should analyze AI content before you act on it or use it, and you should validate your sources to check whether the content is accurate.

A Government of Canada guide on generative AI gives the same kind of warning. These tools can produce content that looks well developed and reasonable but is inaccurate, incomplete, or not consistent with the facts. The guide calls some of that content a hallucination. Training data can also be out of date or leave out many views, so the answer may be biased or missing important context.

Useful habits from those official pages:

  1. Do not treat an AI answer as the final word.
  2. Check important facts against a trusted source, such as an official government page, your council, your school, or another source you already trust.
  3. If the tool does not show sources you can open and check, do not use it as if it were a search engine.
  4. If you cannot tell whether the answer is right, do not use it for a decision that matters — money, health, legal questions, or someone else’s rights.

Get Cyber Safe notes that AI tools often present their content as true facts even when it is not. That can lead people to spread false information without meaning to. Pause, check, and then decide.

This course cannot check an answer for you. You stay responsible for what you send, post, or act on.

lessons.title: Protect your privacy with AI chatbots
lessons.html:
An AI chatbot is a tool that answers in writing (or sometimes by voice) after you type or speak a prompt. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) says the information you put into a chatbot may be collected and stored. Put your privacy first.

The OPC’s key tips are:

  • Limit the personal information you share about yourself.
  • Do not share sensitive or identifiable personal information.
  • Change personal details if you must give an example — for instance, use a made-up name and change anything that could identify a real person.
  • If the chatbot allows it, consider deleting your chat history.
  • Review and adjust your privacy settings, and use strong passwords.
  • Do not share personal information about other people.
  • Never share pictures or personal information of minors (children and young people under 18).

The OPC also lists risks. The information may be stored. The company may not clearly explain how it is used, stored, or shared. It may be used to train the AI system further. It may be used to create profiles about you or to make decisions about you. Future uses may not be clear. A chatbot could even disclose information it has learned about you to other users.

The Cyber Centre adds a similar warning: people may put sensitive personal information into AI prompts without thinking. Threat actors could use that information to impersonate someone or spread false information. Do not share private information with an AI tool unless you understand what it does with your data. Avoid putting personally identifiable information into prompts. See whether the tool lets you delete your prompt history.

This course does not tell you which chatbot to use. If you do use one, share as little as you can.

lessons.title: AI can make scams look more real
lessons.html:
Threat actors use AI in scams. The Cyber Centre says content that is not clearly labelled as AI-generated can spread false information and confusion. AI also helps criminals write phishing messages more often, more automatically, and in a more polished way. A realistic scam message can lead to identity theft, financial fraud, or other cybercrime.

Get Cyber Safe says phishing is still a common way criminals trick people. AI can make those messages look more legitimate, with fewer of the spelling mistakes people used to watch for. It can also use details from social media to make a message feel personal. Red flags that still matter include requests for money, suspicious links or attachments, and email addresses or web names that do not look right.

Get Cyber Safe also describes vishing, or voice phishing. AI can copy the sound of a real person’s voice, including a family member or friend. The page says more of these calls have been reported in Canada, including calls that pretend a loved one is in trouble and needs money or information right away. Stay calm. If anyone calls with an urgent demand for money or personal information, check who they are through another method — for example, hang up and call the person or the organization using a number you already trust. Get Cyber Safe says no law enforcement or government organization in Canada will demand money or sensitive information over the phone. Your bank will not email or call to ask for your password, one-time passcode, card number, or similar secrets.

AI can also create new images and videos that do not exist anywhere else, so an old “search for this picture” check may not prove they are real. If something seems too good to be true, it probably is.

lessons.title: Everyday habits that help you stay safer
lessons.html:
You do not need to become a cyber-security expert. Official Canadian pages point to simple habits.

The Cyber Centre says individuals should practise basic cyber security hygiene: stay informed, use strong passwords, turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA), keep software up to date, use antivirus software, and avoid public Wi-Fi networks. It also suggests posting less personal information online, not opening attachments or links from unknown sources, and using another verified way to communicate if something feels off.

When you look at pictures, videos, or text, Get Cyber Safe lists signs that content may have been made by AI:

  • Images: missing or misplaced objects or body parts (especially hands), odd shadows or lighting, text that does not make sense, or skin and fabric that look unusually smooth or glossy. Some tools add a watermark or small logo.
  • Videos: unnatural movement, people who do not blink, strange shadows, blurs, or light flickers, and voices that sound flat, choppy, or paired with odd background noise.
  • Text: a dry, “robotic” tone, information that is out of date, or the same words repeated again and again.

These signs are clues, not proof. AI is changing, and some fakes will be hard to spot. Always check the source. If a message asks you to send money, click a link, or share personal information, pause.

Do not treat this course as approval to use any one AI product. Check answers, protect privacy, and verify unexpected requests. If you want more practice on email and passwords, your council may also offer the Range Path course on email and online safety.
